html:
From the late 19th century the island of Fernando Po (Bioko) in Spanish Guinea was turned over to cocoa plantations, owned by Spaniards and by the Creole Fernandinos.

The native Bubi were too few for the work, so planters brought contract labourers from Liberia and later from Nigeria. In 1930 a League of Nations inquiry found that Liberian officials had shipped men to the island under force, a scandal that brought down the Liberian president. After that most workers came from southeastern Nigeria, and Nigerian migrants and their pidgin English became part of island life.

Cocoa made Bioko far richer than the mainland province of Río Muni. The trade collapsed after independence, when Nigerian workers left under Macías Nguema, until oil replaced it.
sum: From the late 19th century the island of Fernando Po (Bioko) in Spanish Guinea was turned over to cocoa plantations, owned by Spaniards and by the Creole Fernandinos.
